overview:
The peace offering may come from the herd, the sheep, or the goats, male or female, as long as it is without blemish. As before, the worshiper lays his hand on its head and kills it at the door of the tent, and the priests splash the blood around the altar. Then the chapter turns precise: the fat over the entrails, the two kidneys with their fat, and the lobe above the liver are removed and burned, and from a sheep the whole fat tail as well. A closing rule reaches every home: Israel must eat neither fat nor blood.

Notice what the chapter leaves out. It lists only what goes to the altar and never says what becomes of the meat. That comes later (7:15–21, 31–34): the priest takes the breast and right shoulder, and the worshiper eats the rest. This is the one offering whose meat the giver himself eats.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars assign Leviticus to a priestly writer or school.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The close of the speech from the tent that begins at 1:1, in the second year after the Exodus (Exodus 40:17). Traditional date about 1446 BC; many scholars prefer the 13th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Leviticus 7:11–34 completes these rules: thanksgiving, vow, and freewill kinds, time limits, and the priests' portions. Abel brings the firstlings of his flock “and of the fat thereof” (Genesis 4:4; Moses 5:20).

hermeneutics:
Ritual texts from Ugarit on the Syrian coast (13th century BC) again and again pair two sacrifices: *šrp*, a burnt offering, and *šlmm*, a name from the same root as Hebrew *shelamim*, the peace offering. Leviticus 1 and 3 name a pair that Israel's neighbors already knew. What Leviticus adds is a precise division of the animal: the fat to the altar, the breast and shoulder to the priest, and the rest to the worshiper's table.

Greeks also gave the gods the fat. In Hesiod's *Theogony* (c. 700 BC), Prometheus divides an ox at Mecone, hiding the meat in the stomach and dressing the bones in shining fat for Zeus. Zeus chooses the fat, and Hesiod says this is why men burn white bones to the gods on fragrant altars. Leviticus 3 shares the custom but not the story of a trick. Fat is the choice portion, called “the food of the offering” (vv. 11, 16), and “all the fat is the LORD's.” The worshiper may not eat any of it (v. 17).

In Mesopotamia the sheep's liver was a book of omens. Thirty-two clay liver models from the palace at Mari, inscribed with omens, trained diviners to read its marks, and Ezekiel pictures the king of Babylon who “looked in the liver” (Ezekiel 21:21). Leviticus sends the lobe above the liver to the fire (vv. 4, 10, 15) and says nothing about examining it.

breakdown.label: From the herd, male or female: hand, slaughter, blood
Fat, kidneys, and liver lobe burned on the burnt offering
From the flock: a lamb, the hand, the blood
The lamb's fat and whole tail: “the food of the offering”
A goat: the same portions; “all the fat is the LORD's”
A perpetual statute: eat neither fat nor blood

structure.summary: Sequence: three parallel cases, herd, lamb, goat, then a closing statute (v. 17). No chiasm.

rows.text: Statute for all generations: no fat, no blood

notes: **Repeated list:** the inventory of fat, kidneys, and liver lobe is given three times almost word for word (vv. 3–4, 9–10, 14–15), so the reader learns it by heart.
**Key word:** the Hebrew *chelev*, “fat,” occurs twelve times. It builds to “all the fat is the LORD's” (v. 16) and the ban of v. 17.
**Food:** of chs. 1–3, only ch. 3 calls the altar portion *lechem*, “food” or “bread” (vv. 11, 16).

Chapter 3 closes the speech that began at 1:1 with three gifts a worshiper brings by choice. Each ends its cases with “a sweet savour” (3:5, 16). At 4:1 a new speech begins, and the subject shifts to offerings that sin requires.

**Backward and forward:** at Sinai young men “sacrificed peace offerings of oxen” to seal the covenant (Exodus 24:5). Leviticus 17:5 later requires that animals slaughtered in the open field be brought to the tent as peace offerings.

traditions.text: Moses 5 says Abel hearkened unto the voice of the Lord, and he brings the firstlings of his flock “and of the fat thereof.” The Lord has respect to his offering and not to Cain's. The fat that Leviticus 3 claims for the altar is already the choice gift in the first sacrifice scripture describes. Joseph Smith quoted the verse in 1840, arguing that sacrifices acceptable to God must be offered by those he has authorized, and that Abel magnified the priesthood he received.
traditions.cite: Moses 5:17, 20; Genesis 4:4; Instruction on Priesthood, c. 5 Oct. 1840, p. 4

traditions.text: Abinadi tells the priests of Noah that Israel was given “a law of performances and of ordinances,” to be kept strictly from day to day to keep them in remembrance of God. He adds that all these things were types of things to come. The detailed portions of Leviticus 3 belong to that law of daily remembrance.

Rashi gives two reasons for the name *shelamim*, from the word for peace. The offerings bring peace into the world. Or, following the Sifra, there is peace among all who share them: the altar receives the fat, the priests the breast and shoulder, and the owners the rest, so no one envies another.

Philo admits he has often wondered why the law takes the fat, the kidneys, and the liver lobe and not the heart or brain, where the mind lives. His answer is that the organ from which the mind went astray should not come to the altar of pardon. He adds that once the victim is offered it belongs to God, who makes the worshipers “partakers at the altar and messmates” at his own feast.

The Mishnah ranks peace offerings among the offerings of lesser holiness. They may be slaughtered anywhere in the temple court and eaten anywhere in Jerusalem, by any ritually pure person, cooked any way, for two days and the night between. The priests' share may be eaten by their wives, children, and servants.

The ban of v. 17 was taken with full seriousness. The Mishnah lists thirty-six offenses that carry *karet*, being cut off, when done on purpose, and eating forbidden fat and eating blood are both on the list. Leviticus 7:25 and 17:10 had already threatened the same penalty.

Josephus describes the thank offering of his day. The worshipers lay the kidneys, the caul, all the fat, the lobe of the liver, and the lamb's rump on the altar, and give the breast and right shoulder to the priests. They feast on the rest for two days and burn what remains.

Rabbis in the name of Rabbi Menahem of Galya taught that in the age to come every offering will cease except the thanksgiving offering, the joyful kind of peace offering (7:12). Likewise every prayer will cease except thanksgiving. They cite Jeremiah's promise that the sound of joy and of those bringing thank offerings will be heard again in Jerusalem.

Paul points to Israel's sacrificial meals: “are not they which eat of the sacrifices partakers of the altar?” Eating a peace offering made the eater a sharer with the altar and with the God it belonged to, just as the meat on a pagan table bound its eaters to the idol. Paul draws the conclusion for the Lord's supper: a Christian cannot share the Lord's table and the table of devils.

The Jerusalem council asks Gentile believers to abstain, among other things, from blood and things strangled. The blood rule goes back to Genesis 9:4 and is repeated as a perpetual statute in v. 17 and in Leviticus 17:10–14. The fat rule of the same verse is not included, so the council kept half of the statute and set the other half aside for Gentiles.

Hebrews says Christians have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat. It then names the offerings believers can bring: the sacrifice of praise, the fruit of their lips, and doing good and sharing. The thanksgiving offering, a kind of peace offering (Leviticus 7:12), lies behind the phrase.

Writing to Corinth about church order, Clement notes that the daily sacrifices, peace offerings, sin offerings, and trespass offerings were not offered just anywhere. They were brought only in Jerusalem, at the altar before the temple, after the high priest and ministers had examined the victim. He uses Leviticus as a model of worship done in its proper place and order.
